segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let every person be subject to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been appointed by God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So whoever opposes the authority has resisted what God has appointed, and those who have resisted will bring judgment on themselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For rulers are not a cause of fear to good conduct but to evil. Do you want not to fear the authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for it is God's servant for your good. But if you do evil, be afraid, for it does not carry the sword for nothing. It is God's servant, an avenger bringing wrath on the one who practices evil.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore it is necessary to be subject, not only because of the wrath but also because of conscience.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This is also why you pay taxes, for they are God's officials, devoting themselves to this very thing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pay to all what is owed: tax to whom tax is owed, customs to whom customs, fear to whom fear, honor to whom honor.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Owe no one anything, except to love one another; for the one who loves the other has fulfilled the law.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not murder,” “You shall not steal,” “You shall not covet,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and any other commandment there is, are summed up in this saying:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Love does no evil to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfillment of the law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And do this knowing the time: it is already the hour for you to wake from sleep, for now our salvation is nearer than when we came to believe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The night is far advanced, and the day has drawn near. So let us throw off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let us walk decently, as in the daytime: not in revelry and drunkenness, not in sleeping around and debauchery, not in strife and jealousy.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Instead, put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh to gratify its desires.

notes.note: The Greek phrase, literally 'every soul', is a Septuagint idiom in which 'soul' simply means an individual human being. Older English versions kept 'soul', which now suggests an inner or immaterial part of a person. Most modern translations render it 'everyone' or 'every person'.

The phrase was ordinary language for civic and imperial officials, and the following verses (rulers, the sword, taxes) show that Paul means them. A minority of scholars have argued that angelic powers standing behind the state are also in view, but few accept this today. Verses 1 and 2 play on one Greek root, used for 'be subject', 'appointed', 'opposes' and 'what God has appointed'; English can keep only part of this.

The words pick up 12:19, where believers are told not to avenge themselves but to leave room for 'the wrath', because vengeance belongs to God. Paul now presents the governing authority as one channel of that wrath, which is why verse 5 speaks of 'the wrath' with the article. The sword stands for the authority's power to punish by force; whether it refers specifically to capital punishment is debated.

The word denoted someone who performed a public service, and in the Septuagint it was also used of those serving in the temple. 'Ministers' now suggests clergy to most readers, so 'officials' is used. Whether Paul intends a sacred overtone here is uncertain. Most interpreters take the sense to be civic, with the genitive 'God's' supplying the theological point.

notes.phrase: tax to whom tax is owed, customs to whom customs
notes.traditional: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom
notes.note: The first word refers to direct taxes or tribute levied on subject peoples, the second to indirect charges such as customs duties and tolls. The Roman historian Tacitus records public complaints about the collection of indirect taxes in Rome during the 50s, close to the time of this letter. The repeated 'owed' sets up the play on 'owe' in verse 8.

notes.traditional: respect to whom respect is owed
notes.note: Many modern translations soften this to 'respect', while older versions have 'fear'. 'Fear' is kept because it is the same word used in verses 3 and 4, where it plainly means fear. Some interpreters, comparing 1 Peter 2:17, think the one owed fear is God and not the ruler; the Greek does not decide.

notes.phrase: the one who loves the other has fulfilled the law
notes.traditional: he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law
notes.note: The Greek could also be read 'the one who loves has fulfilled the other law', taking 'other' with 'law' (for example, the Mosaic law as distinct from civil obligations). Nearly all translators and commentators take 'the other' as the object of 'loves', meaning the other person, and that reading is followed here.

notes.traditional: Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness
notes.note: Many later manuscripts add 'You shall not bear false witness' after 'You shall not steal', and the King James Version includes it. The earliest witnesses lack it, and it is generally regarded as a scribal addition to fill out the list from the Ten Commandments. The final quotation is Leviticus 19:18.

Manuscripts divide between two verbs here: one meaning 'throw off' and one meaning 'lay aside' or 'take off', as with clothing. The SBLGNT prints the former; the other major critical edition prints the latter. The sense is little affected.

The Greek word covers military equipment in general and often means 'weapons', as it probably does in 2 Corinthians 6:7 and 10:4. 'Armor' is kept here because the verb is 'put on', the language of clothing that runs through verses 12 to 14. 'Weapons of light' is an equally possible rendering.

The Greek word means 'bed' and, in the plural as here, is a euphemism for sexual encounters. 'Sexual immorality' is the usual English for a different and broader Greek word, so an English idiom that keeps the bed image and the plural sense is used instead. The word paired with it, rendered 'debauchery', denotes conduct without restraint or shame.
